title: Rich Rebuilds gets a $4,100 wrecked Lucid Air moving, and hands it to Lucid
dek: A dead, crashed Lucid Air bought cheap during the bankruptcy scare is driving again, and Lucid's lawyers are deciding what happens next.

car.trim: Year and trim not reported (2022 is a placeholder); all-wheel drive, sold new near $140,000

source.where: Auction car from Florida; the auction house is not named in the coverage
source.boughtNote: Stated by Rich Benoit: $4,100 is in the title of his August 25, 2026 video and in coverage of his first video (Supercar Blondie, MotorBiscuit).
source.title: salvage
source.damage: Crash damage to panels on most of the car, front bumper nearly gone, all wheels curbed; snapped axle, broken ball joint and control arms, shredded tire; crushed coolant line to the front motor; forklift scrapes under the battery; dead low- and high-voltage systems and a locked parking brake. Airbags not deployed.

episodes.t: Lucid's Lawyers Called Me After I Bought Their $140,000 Car for $4,100
episodes.what: The team fits used suspension parts and a coolant line from a donor Lucid, and the low-voltage systems wake up, but the high-voltage battery stops charging; Benoit says Lucid's legal team contacted him.

episodes.t: Lucid Wants My $140,000 Car Back After I Fixed It
episodes.what: Lucid offers to collect his car and a fan's and reset them out of service mode if they can drive onto its trailer, so Benoit forces a charge and gets his Air driving at 35 mph.

parts.why: The crash snapped the original axle

parts.part: Used upper and lower control arms
parts.why: Suspension damaged in the crash; taken from a Lucid hit on the opposite side
Crushed in the crash, leaking coolant; donor part trimmed to fit
A used hub from a rear-drive Air did not fit
Original bumper nearly missing; new parts hard to get, so used pieces were cut and joined
Refill after the leak, done with a vacuum filler instead of Lucid's software

time: About ten weeks and at least three videos so far: the first in late July 2026, then August 25 and October 5, 2026. Unloading the dead car alone took two days. No shop hours given.

costs.note: Only the $4,100 price is stated. Parts ($2,500) is our estimate for used donor-car suspension, cooling, hub and bumper parts plus fluids; no part prices have been published. Labor is the builder's own and isn't counted. Transport and any Lucid fees are unknown and not counted.

value.basis: Clean-title Airs: a 2023 Air Pure sold on Cars & Bids for $31,750 (October 2026); dealers were asking $24,995 to $39,999 for 2022 Grand Tourings and $36,998 for a 2024 Touring. Take 20 to 40 percent off for a rebuilt title (J.D. Power) and you get about $15,000 to $25,000 if Lucid fully unlocks the car. If it stays in service mode with no updates, it is worth about what salvage Airs brought this summer ($6,500 to $8,000, per Supercar Blondie), so the low end is $8,000.

verdict: For $4,100 plus a pile of used parts, Benoit has a moving Lucid Air and a story Lucid can't ignore, so the video side has already paid. The car is less certain. A rebuilt-title Air that Lucid releases and keeps updating could be worth $15,000 to $25,000 against clean-title cars now in the $25,000 to $40,000 range. One stuck in service mode is worth little more than the $6,500 to $8,000 salvage Airs have been bringing. The build shows that on a software-locked EV the maker's servers decide the car's value as much as the wrench work does.
body:
## The buy

Rich Benoit, the Massachusetts YouTuber behind Rich Rebuilds, started this project in late July 2026 with a dead Lucid Air that he says cost him $4,100. Lucid sold cars like it new for something approaching $140,000 [3][5]. The car came out of Florida. The price is Benoit's own: it is in the title of his August 25 episode [1], and reporting on his first video repeats it [3][4]. None of the coverage names the auction house, the model year or the trim, so this file doesn't either.

The price came from the market's mood as much as the car's condition. In mid-July 2026 a rumor spread that Lucid had hired restructuring advisers ahead of a Chapter 11 filing. Lucid denied it and its majority owner, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, backed the company, but the stock fell sharply and salvage Lucid prices fell with it [4]. Supercar Blondie reported that a 2024 Air with a few thousand miles had sold at auction for about $8,000 and a 2023 for $6,500 [3]. Benoit called his buy "pennies on the dollar for one of the most advanced electric vehicles in America" [4].

## The damage

The car would not wake up. Its electronic parking brake had locked the rear wheels, and neither jump packs, a 14-volt supply nor a diesel generator could bring it to life. The crew winched the roughly 5,000-pound car off the transporter on plastic trays greased with baby oil and Crisco, and it took them two days [3][5]. Under it they found:

- dented or wrecked panels nearly all the way round, including the front clamshell, doors and quarter panels; the front bumper was close to missing, and all four wheels were curbed [4][5];
- a snapped axle, a broken ball joint and other suspension damage, plus a shredded tire [4][5];
- a coolant leak near the battery, later traced to a crushed coolant line to the front drive motor [3][7];
- forklift scrapes on the underside. The battery enclosure appeared intact [3][4].

The airbags had not deployed and the cabin was clean apart from blood on the steering wheel from the original crash [4][5]. On the Lucid Owners forum, where the build was followed from the first video, the car was described as one that had been "in a major accident and sat for multiple years" [11].

## The work and the parts

The first round of work was electrical. Benoit released the parking brake by putting 12 volts straight onto its motor, without Lucid's software, and found several small low-voltage batteries hidden around the car that still held a charge [5]. In the August 25 episode the team fitted a used axle, upper and lower control arms and a coolant line taken from another Lucid that had been hit on the opposite side. They trimmed the hose to make it fit and filled the cooling system with a vacuum tool, again without factory diagnostics. A used hub from a rear-drive Air turned out not to fit, so they had to find the right one [7]. The low-voltage systems came back. The high-voltage battery started to charge, then stopped, and would not start again [7][8].

The October 5 episode solved that with what Benoit called a "trick force feed" that got the high-voltage side to take a charge. The team also bypassed parking brake faults and topped up leaking coolant. Body parts were so hard to get that they cut used bumper pieces in half and joined them with plastic staples and hot glue [9][10]. By the end of that video Benoit had his car driving at 35 mph [9][10].

## The money and the lawyers

The fight with Lucid over salvage cars was the bigger story. Before Benoit's second car arrived, a fan's lightly damaged Air with a salvage title had been quoted about $20,000 in parts and nearly 190 hours of labor to "re-shell" it, close to $50,000 in all, before anyone at Lucid looked at it. Lucid would not sell that owner's body shop the cosmetic parts. Until the car passed Lucid's process, it stayed in a service mode capped at walking pace [6]. Benoit argued that blocking over-the-air updates for these cars leaves owners "driving an unsafe vehicle just because of Lucid's policy" [6].

On August 11 Benoit said Lucid had contacted him and that lawyers were involved [11]. In the October video he said the email "wasn't a cease and desist" [9]. Lucid offered to collect his car and the fan's car, take them out of service and "turtle" mode and reset their errors, on one condition: both cars had to drive onto Lucid's trailer under their own power. Benoit said "Lucid won't take any dead cars" [9][10]. Torque News and FastLane Only reported that Lucid told him it is reviewing third-party repair and plans better access to tools for independent shops, though Lucid's published service material still points to its own centers and approved body shops [7][8].

Money spent beyond the $4,100 isn't public. Most parts came used from a donor car, and none of the reporting gives what they cost.

## What's next

Benoit said "It's in Lucid's hands now" [9]. Both cars were driven onto the trailer and Lucid agreed to collect them [10]. What matters next is whether Lucid gives his Air back fully unlocked, with software updates and charging working, or whether it stays a salvage car the factory treats as a parts problem. Either way the title stays branded. Clean-title Airs are cheap now: a 2023 Air Pure sold on Cars & Bids for $31,750 this October [13], and dealers were asking $24,995 to $39,999 for 2022 Grand Tourings and $36,998 for a 2024 Touring [12][14]. Rebuilt-title cars usually sell for 20 to 40 percent less than clean ones [16].
